analysis.one_liner: Keeps most medical debt off credit reports and stops collectors for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one Democrat with zero cosponsors, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, and never got a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar credit bureaus from putting medical debt from medically necessary care on credit reports at all, and would block other medical debt from appearing for a year after collection begins. It would also make debt collectors wait two years before trying to collect a medical bill, and would require anyone reporting a medical debt to first warn the patient about these protections. Patients who pay or settle a bill within that window could never have it reported.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with medical debt — roughly, anyone who ends up owing a hospital, doctor, or ambulance company. Today an unpaid medical bill sent to a collector can sit on a credit report for years and drag down credit scores, making mortgages, car loans, rentals, and jobs harder to get. This bill would keep medically necessary debt off credit reports entirely, shield other medical debt for its first year in collections, stop collection calls and lawsuits on medical bills for two years, and give patients notice and a chance to apply for financial assistance or insurance coverage before anything is reported. People with low incomes or documented hardship would get extra time determined by the consumer protection bureau.

how_it_helps.text: Bars credit bureaus from including medical debt from medically necessary procedures — including preventive care like cancer screenings, flu shots, and mammograms — on credit reports at all [S2, S3].
Keeps other medical debt off credit reports for its first 365 days, and blocks it permanently if the patient or an insurer pays or settles it within that window [S2, S3].

Makes it an unfair practice for debt collectors to pursue a medical bill before two years have passed since the first payment was due, giving patients time to resolve insurance disputes or apply for aid [S2, S3].

Requires anyone furnishing medical debt information to first send the patient a notice explaining when and whether the debt can be reported, and telling them they can check insurance coverage or apply for financial assistance [S2, S3].
Lets the consumer protection bureau give additional time to borrowers demonstrating hardship, defined as people facing severe financial or personal barriers that leave them unable to repay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Debt collectors would lose two years of leverage over medical debt; credit bureaus would lose a large category of reportable data; and hospitals and other providers would lose credit reporting and third-party collections as tools for getting paid, which could push them to demand payment upfront or pursue patients directly. Providers and collectors who profit from medical debt collections would bear the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Debt collectors, credit bureaus, medical providers

drawbacks.text: Hospitals and medical providers would lose credit reporting and third-party collection agencies as tools for recovering unpaid bills, and some could respond by demanding payment upfront or refusing care from patients with unpaid balances, which would land hardest on people without insurance [S2, S3].

A blanket two-year ban on collecting any medical debt is broad: it covers debts that are legitimately owed and undisputed, and honest supporters would acknowledge that some providers and collectors face real losses on bills patients are able but unwilling to pay [S2, S3].
The bill does not reduce the underlying medical bills themselves; it only delays and limits their consequences, so patients would still owe the money [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefits are substantial: medical debt is a leading cause of credit damage and financial distress, and the bill would shield them from it on both the credit-report and collections fronts while giving them notice and time to seek aid. The costs fall on the collections and credit reporting industries and, indirectly, on providers, who might tighten payment practices for uninsured patients. The bill is one-sided — it does nothing to lower medical prices or bills themselves — but its main effects clearly favor patients over creditors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, sat there with no hearing and no vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on March 23, 2023 [S1, S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
Not a single member of the House signed on as a cosponsor during the two years the bill was pending [S4].
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collectors, credit bureaus, and medical providers that use reporting and collections to recover unpaid bills are better off, because the restrictions never became law and medical debt remains reportable and collectible on the current timetable.

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee chair
against.role: Committee chair who controls the hearing and markup calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration.

against.name: Members of the House
against.what_they_did: None signed on as a cosponsor over the bill's two-year life.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, and no Republican or other Democrat cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape can only be described as a lone Democratic sponsor with no visible support from either party.

industries.note: The bill makes collecting any medical debt an unfair practice for two years after the first payment is due, cutting off a major revenue stream from hospital and doctor bills. Collectors profit by pursuing exactly these debts, so their interest runs directly against patients here.

Credit bureaus would be barred from including medically necessary debt on reports at all and other medical debt for a year, shrinking the data that feeds their scoring products. Their loss is patients' gain in credit access.

Providers would lose credit reporting and third-party collections as tools for getting paid, but patients would also gain time to settle bills, use insurance, or apply for charity care before any collection activity. On balance the bill removes leverage providers currently use against patients.
